newsitem.title: CHINA: Shanghai Yaohua Pilkington glass hits hard times.
newsitem.headline: Shanghai Yaohua Pilkington glass hits hard times.

text.p: Glass-maker Yaohua Pilkington, once the bright star of listed joint ventures in Shanghai, has hit hard times with glass prices plunging and no turnaround in sight, analysts said on Tuesday.

The company, in which Pilkington International Holdings has a minority stake, built its fortunes on advanced technology that other firms in China have since emulated, and on a construction boom that has largely faded.

One analyst said profits this year were expected to fall sharply to possibly around 120 million yuan ($14.46 million) from 263 million yuan in 1995 and a company spokesman said this estimate was fairly close to the company's own projections.
The analyst said there was little prospect of a turnaround before 1998 at the earliest and several foreign brokerages in Shanghai said they were recommending Yaohua as a "sell".
"Business is not good this year, mainly because the competition is very tough," said Jin Minli, head of the company's general management office.
"The fall in the price of glass products has had a significant effect. In the first half of this year alone, prices for our glass products fell more than 30 percent," Jin said.

Up to late last year, Shanghai Yaohua had the only production facilities in China for producing glass of a thickness less than 12mm. Three other companies have since come on line with the same capability.

"They are facing fierce competition and pressure," said a stock analyst with a foreign brokerage in Hong Kong. "The domestic real estate market shows no signs of recovering, so demand for glass is not promising. Exports are not promising either due to capacity expanding in Indonesia and South Korea."
Overall, China's construction industry is expected to benefit from the central bank's decision to cut interest rates in May and in August this year.
But the benefits for the glass industry in general and Shanghai Yaohua in particular will be slow in being felt, analysts said.
"The interest rate relaxation is a positive sign but we won't see an impact on the glass market until next year at least, certainly not this year," said the Hong Kong analyst.

Yaohua's Jin said the company was hopeful of a turnaround in 1997, with the construction industry in Shanghai leading the way. But in the meantime it has suspended plans for a third production line until market conditions improve.
"Next year, the situation for our company may see some improvement," Jin said.
"Shanghai has begun construction of its second subway line and is expanding its freeway system. All this infrastructure work will have a positive effect on economic activity overall," she added.
The irony is that Yaohua is viewed by analysts as being one of the best-managed of the 41 B-share companies listed on the Shanghai stock exchange.
"The management is fine, and the technology is good. But the wider market factors are against them," said a Shanghai-based broker. "I don't expect their fortunes to recover until 1998 at least."
